linkup.title: Cisco's latest layoffs could affect hundreds as workforce reduction continues | Ctech
linkup.snippet:
The company says the latest round involves less than 1% of its 82,400 employees, but has not disclosed the exact number. Its headcount has fallen nearly 9% in two years, even as revenue surged 24% in its latest quarter.
The latest cuts come against the backdrop of a sustained decline in Cisco's workforce. Its employee count fell from approximately 90,400 in July 2024 to 86,200 a year later and 82,400 in July 2026, a reduction of about 8,000 people, or nearly 9%.
At the start of fiscal 2027, the company provided an AI agent to every employee, while encouraging broader use of the technology across its operations. The latest round also comes after several years of restructuring. Cisco's filings show that it recorded approximately $2.2 billion in restructuring and other charges across fiscal 2024, 2025 and 2026, as it repeatedly reorganized its business and redirected investment toward priority areas.
Cisco has carried out another round of layoffs, continuing a workforce reduction that has seen the networking giant shed approximately 8,000 employees over the past two years, even as its business expands at its fastest pace in more than a decade. The latest cuts reportedly took place on November 18, according to LinkedIn posts.
Cisco reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24% year over year. CEO Chuck Robbins told analysts last week that the company expected to generate $19 billion in additional revenue compared with two years earlier, despite having fewer employees. ... Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson said the decline in headcount was driving an expected increase of approximately 19% in revenue per employee in fiscal 2027. The November layoffs follow a major restructuring announced in May, when Cisco said it would eliminate nearly 4,000 positions, representing less than 5% of its workforce.

In March 2024, Cisco Systems received unconditional EU antitrust approval for its $28 billion bid for cybersecurity firm Splunk.
On April 28, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court heard a case alleging that Cisco Systems aided the Chinese government in repressing Falun Gong members through its "Golden Shield" surveillance system. Filed in 2011 under the Alien Tort Statute, the lawsuit raises questions about corporate complicity in human rights abuses and the use of technology for government control in China. In 2020, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute accused at least 82 major brands, including Cisco, of being connected to forced Uyghur labor in Xinjiang. In October 2007, employees of Cisco's Brazilian unit were arrested on charges that they had imported equipment without paying import duties.
